facts.text: On this date in 1917, the Bolshevik Revolution began in Petrograd — an event that reshaped a third of the planet's surface for 74 years, yet unfolded with fewer casualties than an average weekend of street crime in modern Caracas.
On this date in 2000, Hillary Clinton became the first First Lady elected to public office, winning a New York Senate seat despite never having lived in the state before 1999.
Mongolia has more horses than people — roughly 4.3 million horses to 3.4 million humans — and a significant share of the population still navigates by landmarks rather than street addresses.
The city of Tokyo governs itself as a "metropolitan prefecture," a legal category that exists nowhere else on Earth, giving it simultaneous powers of both a city and a regional state.
More people live inside a 40-kilometer radius of Jakarta than in the entire country of Australia — a compression of humanity that makes it the most densely consequential urban zone on the planet.
On this day in 1917, the Bolshevik Revolution began — wiping out Russia's entire bond market overnight and defaulting on $12 billion in Tsarist debt, the largest sovereign default the world had seen.
On Nov 7, 2000, Election Night uncertainty froze U.S. futures markets. The S&P 500 swung 5% in after-hours trading before anyone knew who the next president would be.
The New York Stock Exchange was founded in 1792 under a buttonwood tree. The original members agreed to charge each other fixed commissions — an illegal cartel by modern standards.
Saudi Aramco's 2019 IPO raised $25.6 billion, the largest in history. It briefly made Aramco worth $2 trillion — more than Apple, Google, and Amazon combined at the time.
The entire global derivatives market is estimated at over $600 trillion in notional value — roughly six times the annual economic output of every country on Earth.
On this date in 1867, Marie Curie was born — the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, and whose notebooks remain too radioactive to handle safely 150 years later.

On Nov 7, 1996, NASA launched Mars Global Surveyor, which discovered that Mars has a fractured magnetic field — suggesting its core solidified unevenly, a planetary death unlike anything in our solar system.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A single teaspoon of its material would weigh about a billion tons on Earth.
Your body contains roughly 37 trillion cells, yet only 43% of them are human — the rest are microbial, meaning you are, by cell count, more microbe than person.
Light takes 8 minutes to reach Earth from the Sun, but the photons themselves took up to 100,000 years to escape the Sun's core through repeated absorption and re-emission before that final sprint.
On this day in 1917, the Bolshevik Revolution began — an event Lenin had rehearsed mentally for 12 years, yet which unfolded in under 24 hours, almost by accident.
Oxford University was teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. It held classes in 1096; Tenochtitlán wasn't founded until 1325.
On this day in 1944, FDR won his fourth presidential term — a feat now constitutionally impossible, sealed by an amendment passed partly because of him.
The fax machine was invented in 1843, 33 years before the telephone. Alexander Bain patented it while most of the world still traveled by horse.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. The pyramid is that old.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012. Already feels ancient.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh longing for a home that may never have existed. Untranslatable — English needs four words just to approximate it.
On this day in 1917, the Bolshevik Revolution began. The Russian word 'toska' — a soul-ache with no cause, pure yearning — may be the most honest word the century produced.
Apricity (n.): the warmth of sun in winter. English had this word in 1623 and abandoned it. November is exactly when we need it back.

On this day in 1805, Lewis and Clark first saw the Pacific. The Chinook word 'cultus' — meaning worthless, or just for fun — entered Pacific Northwest English and quietly outlasted the expedition's fame.
On this day in 2013, the Bitcoin price crossed $200 for the first time, then doubled to $400 within two weeks — a velocity that wouldn't be matched again until the 2017 ICO mania.
On this day in 2017, Ethereum's EIP-1 governance repo reached 1,000 GitHub stars — a minor milestone that now marks when protocol governance by open PR became the industry default.

Satoshi's known wallet addresses have never moved a single satoshi. The 1.1 million BTC mined in Bitcoin's first year remains untouched, making Satoshi the largest provably dormant creditor in financial history.
Ethereum's EIP-1559 burned over 1 million ETH in its first six months — an annualized deflation rate that briefly made ETH net-deflationary during high-congestion periods post-Merge.

The Bitcoin genesis block contains the text 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks,' timestamping the protocol's ideological origin to the exact day The Times ran that headline: January 3, 2009.

On this date in 2012, Geoff Hinton's team submitted the AlexNet paper to NIPS. It cut the ImageNet error rate by 10 percentage points — a margin so large reviewers assumed a mistake in the submission.

On this date in 2022, Twitter's algorithmic timeline code was open-sourced under Musk's ownership, revealing that tweets from verified accounts received a 4x ranking multiplier baked directly into the model.
GPT-4 was trained on roughly 50 petaflop/s-days of compute. The human brain runs on about 20 watts. The gap in energy efficiency is still around four orders of magnitude.

DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins — essentially the entire known protein universe — in a database released freely in 2022. Structural biology had accumulated ~180,000 entries in the prior 50 years.

The first neural network to beat a human at Go, AlphaGo, was defeated in 2016 by a human amateur using a strategy of placing stones in fixed geometric patterns — a known weakness that later versions were specifically patched to handle.
